title: Production serving: unified narrative & buyer-signal brief
content:
Purpose and target:
This brief is a compact, customer-facing and internal-ready narrative to align messaging across demand gen, sales engineering, product marketing, and solutions engineering. It focuses on the decision signals (buyer questions, risk vectors, and success criteria) that indicate a customer is ready to evaluate Redwood for production LLM serving.

Core thesis (one-sentence):
Companies win on LLM features not by hoarding models but by owning inference: the runtime, economics, and operational controls that make model outputs predictable, inexpensive, and reliable at scale. Redwood is the developer-first inference platform built for production economics.

Mission (short):
Make high-performance, reliable LLM inference accessible and predictable for every engineering team.

Why this matters (problem statement):
- Teams trying to move LLM features into production face three interlocking problems: unpredictable unit cost, brittle latency at scale, and operational complexity (rollouts, fallbacks, caching, and observability).
- Vendor and cloud lock-in, opaque performance claims, and rapid model churn magnify risk for product and infra owners.

Redwood value pillars (top-level messaging):
1) Predictable unit economics: Reduce per-token cost through smart batching, prefix/KV caching, and model-selection policies that are measurable and controllable. Speak in percent improvements and real tradeoffs.
2) Production reliability: Multi-variant fallbacks, regional routing, and SLA-backed capacity mean apps stay responsive under load and incident conditions.
3) Developer-first runtime: One API, consistent SDKs, and an operations console that surfaces token-level cost, latency, and quality regressions.
4) Deployment flexibility: Hosted for speed, Dedicated for predictable capacity, Private for compliance — same interface so teams avoid rework as needs change.

Buyer signals (what to listen for in discovery):
- Product/PM: “We need to ship chat/assist features with <100ms p50 generation latency for short responses.”
- ML/Infra: “We’re seeing token costs spike on peak; we need deterministic cost controls and better KV cache behavior.”
- Platform/SRE: “Can you integrate with our KMS/VPC? We need audit logs and private deployment options.”
- Leader/Finance: “What’s the path to predictable monthly cost when usage grows 10–50x?”

Quick rebut tracks / competitive differentiators (how to respond to common competitor claims):
- Competitor: “Use model hosted APIs — faster to start.”
  Response: Start fast is real; Redwood’s hosted API matches that ease but is backed by production tooling and a roadmap to Dedicated/Private with no API rewrite. The risk we reduce is not time-to-prototype but time-to-safe-scale.
- Competitor: “Run your own inference — you’ll save money.”
  Response: Self-hosting hides operational tax: engineering time, regressions, and unpredictable unit economics. Redwood offers comparable or better economics once you include engineering overhead, plus features like automated batching, KV caching, and kernel selection that are hard to replicate.
- Competitor: “We provide managed endpoints on cloud GPUs.”
  Response: Managed endpoints are a piece; Redwood is a full-stack inference platform with deployment abstraction, smart routing, and quality monitoring tied to prompt sets — not just an endpoint.

Proof points and specificity to use in pitch (numbers you can test/claim internally):
- Typical latency SLO: p50 < 40–80ms for short assistant responses on Dedicated configurations (depends on model & hardware). Call out ranges rather than single numbers.
- Typical cost impact for batchable workloads: 20–60% token-cost reduction with smart batching + prefix caching compared to naive single-request inference.
- Onboarding time: self-serve hosted API < 1 hour to demo; Dedicated proof-of-concept < 4 weeks for a small reserved pool with baseline throughput SLAs.
- Observable evidence: dashboards showing token-level cost, per-route latency heatmaps, and rollback/fallback event traces.

Persona-specific message hooks (short bullets):
- For ML engineers: “We handle KV cache lifecycle, continuous batching, and quantization-friendly runtime choices so your model’s inference is stable and fast across tokens.”
- For infra/platform: “Single control plane for routing, policies, and telemetry across hosted/dedicated/private — integrate with KMS and VPCs without rearchitecting apps.”
- For product teams: “Predictable pricing levers (batching, cache, model variants) let you price features and forecast spend with confidence.”

Sample one-liner and 30-second pitch: 
- One-liner: Redwood Inference is a developer-first inference platform that makes latency, cost, and reliability predictable across hosted, dedicated, and private deployments.
- 30-second: Teams building LLM features hit a ceiling when prototypes scale — costs spike, latency becomes unpredictable, and rollouts break. Redwood removes that ceiling by combining a high-throughput runtime with operational controls: intelligent batching and caching to lower token costs, routing and fallbacks to maintain SLAs, and the same API across hosted, Dedicated, and Private so you can avoid rewrites as you scale.

Competitive map (high-level talking points):
- Lightweight hosted API players: fastest for prototyping, weaker on SLAs/eval tooling. Emphasize Redwood’s hosted parity plus production features.
- Cloud managed endpoints / GPU offerings: infrastructure-focused, fewer inference-first optimizations and less tooling for rollouts and quality telemetry.
- Self-hosted runtimes / open-source stacks: flexible but high ops burden. Redwood bridges the gap with a runtime-level advantage + managed options.

Objections playbook (short):
- Objection: "We already have infra to host models." Response: Ask about total engineering cost and incident history; offer a small POC that benchmarks your workload vs. self-hosted for unit economics and SLIs.
- Objection: "We need full data residency/airgap." Response: Point to Private deployment options and KMS/HSM integrations and offer an architecture review with solutions engineering.

Tactical next steps for GTM teams (recommended experiments):
1) Create a 1-pager for sales with the buyer signals checklist and two proof-point slides (latency ranges, cost ranges).
2) Add three short demo scripts: low-latency chat, high-concurrency batching, and a Dedicated failover scenario.
3) Run 5 competitive win/loss interviews tagged by buyer signal to refine objection rebuttals.

Open questions (for product + SE):
- Which Dedicated configs produce the most repeatable p50/p95 numbers for each model class? Need a benchmark matrix.
- Can we standardize the phrasing and ranges for cost reduction claims by workload archetype?
- What minimal telemetry should we require in a POC to prove "predictable economics" to finance stakeholders?

Draft homepage hero options (short lines to iterate on):
- “Predictable inference, built for production.”
- “Ship LLM features with latency and cost you can forecast.”

Closing / purpose:
This is a working narrative — short, tactical, and engineered for sales/SE enablement. Use this doc to align demos, proof points, and the first 5 customer conversations. Feedback welcome; plan to sync next week to lock specific quantitative claims for public materials.
